{{distinguish|text=[[Simon's problem]] in computational complexity}}
{{Multiple issues|{{Primary sources|date=June 2021}}
{{Context|article|date=June 2021}}}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Simon problems''' (or '''Simon's problems''') are a series of fifteen questions posed in the year 2000 by [[Barry Simon]], an American [[mathematical physicist]].<ref name="simon imperial">{{cite book|last=Simon |first=Barry |chapter=Schrödinger Operators in the Twenty-First Century | title=Mathematical Physics 2000 |pages=283–288 |publisher=[[Imperial College London]] |isbn=978-1-86094-230-3 |doi=10.1142/9781848160224_0014 |year=2000}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Dynamics and Spectral Theory of Quasi-Periodic Schrödinger-type Operators |first1=C. A. |last1=Marx |first2=Svetlana |last2=Jitomirskaya |journal=Ergodic Theory and Dynamical Systems |volume=37 |issue=8 |pages=2353–2393 |year=2017 |arxiv=1503.05740 |doi=10.1017/etds.2016.16|s2cid=119317111 |author-link2=Svetlana Jitomirskaya}}</ref> Inspired by other collections of mathematical problems and open [[conjecture]]s, such as [[Hilbert problems|the famous list]] by [[David Hilbert]], the Simon problems concern [[Operator (physics)#Operators in quantum mechanics|quantum operators]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.math.pku.edu.cn/teachers/gansb/conference09/Damanik-Minicourse-2009-08-09.pdf |title=Dynamics of SL(2,R)-Cocycles and Applications to Spectral Theory; Lecture 1: Barry Simon's 21st Century Problems |first=David |last=Damanik |access-date=2018-07-07 |website=Beijing International Center for Mathematical Research, [[Peking University]]}}</ref> Eight of the problems pertain to the anomalous [[Spectrum (functional analysis)|spectral]] behavior of [[Schrodinger operator|Schrödinger operators]], and five concern operators that incorporate the [[Coulomb potential]].<ref name="simon imperial" /><ref>{{cite web |title=Simon's Problem |url=https://home.cs.colorado.edu/~alko5368/lecturesCSCI3090/lecture11.pdf |website=[[University of Colorado Boulder]]}}</ref> 

In 2014, [[Artur Avila]] won a [[Fields Medal]] for work including the solution of three Simon problems.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www2.cnrs.fr/en/2435.htm?debut=8&theme1=12 |title=Fields Medal awarded to Artur Avila |website=[[Centre national de la recherche scientifique]] |date=2014-08-13 |access-date=2018-07-07}}</ref><ref name="guardian">{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/alexs-adventures-in-numberland/2014/aug/13/fields-medals-2014-maths-avila-bhargava-hairer-mirzakhani |title=Fields Medals 2014: the maths of Avila, Bhargava, Hairer and Mirzakhani explained |website=[[The Guardian]] |last=Bellos |first=Alex |date=2014-08-13 |access-date=2018-07-07|author-link=Alex Bellos}}</ref> Among these was the problem of [[mathematical proof|proving]] the set of [[Energy level|energy levels]] of one particular abstract quantum system was, in fact, the [[Cantor set]], a challenge known as the "[[Ten Martini Problem]]" after the reward [[Mark Kac]] offered for solving it.<ref name="guardian" /><ref>{{cite web|last=Tao |first=Terry |title=Avila, Bhargava, Hairer, Mirzakhani |url=https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2014/08/12/avila-bhargava-hairer-mirzakhani/ |website=What's New |date=2014-08-12 |access-date=2018-07-07 |author-link=Terence Tao}}</ref> 

The 2000 list was a refinement of a similar set of problems Simon had posed in 1984.<ref name="simon birkhauser">{{cite book|last=Simon|first=Barry|url=http://www.math.caltech.edu/SimonPapers/R27.pdf|title=Perspectives in Mathematics: Anniversary of Oberwolfach 1984|publisher=[[Birkhäuser]]|year=1984|pages=423&ndash;454|chapter=Fifteen problems in mathematical physics|access-date=24 June 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last=Coley |first=Alan A. |title=Open problems in mathematical physics |journal=Physica Scripta |volume=92 |issue=9 |pages=093003 |arxiv=1710.02105 |doi=10.1088/1402-4896/aa83c1 |year=2017 |bibcode=2017PhyS...92i3003C |s2cid=3892374 }}</ref>

== Context ==
Background definitions for the "Coulomb energies" problems (<math>N</math> non-relativistic particles ([[electron]]s) in <math>\mathbb{R}^{3}</math> with [[spin (physics)|spin]] <math> 1/2 </math> and an infinitely heavy [[atomic nucleus|nucleus]] with charge <math>Z</math> and Coulombic mutual interaction): 

* <math>\mathcal{H}_f^{(N)}</math> is the space of functions on <math>L^2(\mathbb{R}^{3N}; \mathbb{C}^{2N})</math> which are asymmetrical under exchange of the <math>N</math> spin and space coordinates.<ref name="simon imperial" /> Equivalently, the subspace of <math> (L^2(\mathbb{R}^{3})\otimes  \mathbb{C}^{2})^{\otimes N}</math> which is asymmetrical under the exchange of the <math>N</math> factors.
* The [[Hamiltonian (quantum mechanics)|Hamiltonian]] is <math>H(N, Z) := \sum_{i = 1}^N(-\Delta_i - \frac{Z}{|x_i|} ) + \sum_{i < j}\frac{1}{|x_i - x_j|}</math>. Here <math>x_i \in \mathbb{R}^3 </math> is the coordinate of the  <math>i</math>-th particle, <math>\Delta_i</math> is the [[Laplace operator|Laplacian]] with respect to the coordinate <math>x_i</math>. Even if the Hamiltonian does not explicitly depend on the state of the spin sector, the presence of spin has an effect due to the asymmetry condition on the total wave-function.
* We define <math>E(N, Z) := \min_{\mathcal{H}_f} H(N, Z)</math>, that is, the [[ground state]] energy of the <math>(N,Z)</math> system.
* We define <math>N_0(Z)</math> to be the smallest value of <math>N</math> such that <math>E(N + j, Z) = E(N, Z)</math> for all positive [[integer]]s <math>j</math>; it is known such a number always exists and is always between <math>Z</math> and <math>2Z</math>, inclusive.<ref name="simon imperial" />

In 2000, Simon claimed five of the problems he listed (namely 1B, 9A, 10B, 10C and 10D, 12D) were solved.<ref name="simon imperial" />
